title: Drinking to death: Hyponatraemia induced by synthetic phenethylamines

claims.statement: After MDMA, a fall in blood sodium (below 130 mmol/L) with seizures and brain swelling has been reported in mostly young people within hours of taking the drug, in two case series from poison services and in published case reports. These describe a pattern but cannot say how often it happens, because they count only people who became ill and came to a poison service or hospital. In 17 patients aged 15 to 26 (7 men, 10 women) reported to a UK poisons service over 28 months (Hartung et al., 2002), sodium on the first day was 107 to 128 mmol/L and all had become ill within 12 hours of taking the drug. A large amount of fluid, alcoholic or not, was known to have been drunk by 10 of the 17 (8 of the 15 who recovered and both who died; editors' count); for 5 of the 15 who recovered the fluid history was not available. Of those 15, 10 had seizures and 13 were recorded as recovering completely; of the 13 with a stated amount of MDMA, 12 had taken 2 or fewer tablets (half a tablet to three), and temperature at hospital was recorded as normal in 12 (37.5 degrees Celsius in two, 34.8 in one). Two patients died after brain swelling, a 15-year-old and an 18-year-old, both female, each after one tablet and each having taken MDMA before: one had drunk at least 3 litres of water while dancing, the other water from about two hours after the tablet, with some alcohol; both were given or drank more water after they began to feel ill, arrived at hospital at 32.6 and 33 degrees, and had blood MDMA of 0.05 and 0.209 mg/l. The UK authors note that people had at first been advised to drink plenty of fluids to prevent overheating. In California poison-centre records for 2000 to 2005 (Rosenson et al., 2007), 73 of 188 people with a recorded sodium (about 39 in 100) had a level below 130 mmol/L; 13 of the 545 included cases died, 4 of them in the low-sodium group, all with brain swelling on CT scan and low blood pressure needing medicines. Hyperthermia was recorded in 40 of the 545 (7.3 in 100) and did not differ clearly between people with and without low sodium (odds ratios 0.58 in women and 0.29 in men, both intervals including 1). In that series MDMA exposure rests on the history given (35 of 103 urine screens were negative for amphetamines but still counted), and the paper gives neither the amount of fluid nor the amount of MDMA. A narrative review of published case reports (Campbell & Rosner, 2008; second-hand, and its table of 32 cases draws 10 rows from the California series) describes more than 25 reports with sodium 101 to 130 mEq/L, most in females aged 15 to 30 after a single dose, including one in which sodium fell from 136 to 130 after 1700 ml of water was drunk following five tablets. A later narrative review (Faria et al., 2020; second-hand, from a PubMed search to October 2019 run mainly by one author) tabulates 52 published cases from 1991 to 2018, 21 of them deaths, with sodium of 101 to 130 mmol/L in the 36 rows that give one, but its table has errors: it appears to list two patients twice, cites an unrelated laboratory-methods paper for one case, includes three deaths with no low sodium recorded, leaves one death's outcome blank and draws 10 of its 21 deaths from the California series, so it adds no independent count. The amount taken is unknown or blank in 30 of its 52 rows, although that review, like the earlier one, says most cases followed a single dose; and in its 10 deaths with a sodium value, sodium (109 to 126 mmol/L) lay within the range of those who recovered (editors' count). The papers explain the fall by MDMA making the body release the water-holding hormone vasopressin, so that water is held back and drinking beyond the body's needs dilutes the sodium; the hormone rise is described from other studies not read here, and the UK authors write that the mechanism remains to be established. None of the papers read here compared amounts of MDMA or of fluid between people, and the 2020 review cites no study that measured how much people drank, so they cannot show whether taking more changes the risk. Blood sodium was not measured in the controlled laboratory sessions of healthy volunteers (Vizeli & Liechti, 2017).
claims.magnitude: UK poisons service, 17 patients over 28 months (Hartung): day 1 sodium 107 to 128 mmol/l; symptoms within 12 hours of the drug in all; large fluid intake known in 10 (8 of the 15 who recovered and both who died), history not available for 5 of the 15; seizures in 10 of the 15 who recovered; 13 of the 15 recorded as recovering completely; temperature at hospital normal in 12 of 15 (37.5 in two, 34.8 in one); 12 of 13 with a stated amount took 2 or fewer tablets (half a tablet to 3); 6 with biochemistry typical of excess antidiuretic hormone; 2 deaths (aged 15 and 18, both female, one tablet each, blood MDMA 0.05 and 0.209 mg/l, temperature 32.6 and 33 degrees Celsius at hospital). California poison control, 545 included cases 2000 to 2005 (Rosenson): sodium recorded in 188 (34.5%); below 130 mmol/L in 73 (about 39 in 100; the text once says 74), median 122 (25th to 75th percentile 119 to 124); 13 deaths in 545 (2.4%), 4 of them in the low-sodium group, all with brain swelling on CT and low blood pressure needing medicines; hyperthermia in 40 of 545 (7.3%), odds ratio for hyperthermia with low sodium against without 0.58 (0.15 to 2.17) in women and 0.29 (0.04 to 2.40) in men; rave party the recorded site for 50 of 545 (9.1%), including 3 of 74 low-sodium cases. Narrative review (Campbell), second-hand: more than 25 case reports, sodium 101 to 130 mEq/L; 32 tabulated cases, 16 deaths. Narrative review (Faria), second-hand: Table 3, 52 rows 1991–2018 (editors' count: 46 women, 21 deaths, 27 recoveries; sodium 101–130 mmol/L in 36 rows, 109–126 in the 10 deaths with a value; amount unknown or blank in 30 rows), with probable duplicates (about 50 distinct cases), an untraceable citation, 3 fatal rows without recorded low sodium and 10 deaths from the California series. No rate of low sodium among people who take MDMA can be derived from these counts.

claims.statement: Among people reported to California poison control in 2000 to 2005 with ecstasy intoxication and a recorded blood sodium (188 of 545 cases; Rosenson et al., 2007), low sodium (below 130 mmol/L) was found in 55 of 105 women (52 in 100) and 18 of 83 men (22 in 100), an odds ratio of 3.97 (95% CI 2.08 to 7.59), which is 31 more in 100 women than men among those tested (editors' calculation); sodium was recorded about as often in women (35 in 100) as in men (33 in 100). Within each sex, women with low sodium had higher odds of coma (odds ratio 3.93, 1.20 to 12.90) and of seizure (4.38, 1.74 to 11.00) than women without it, while in men the intervals for coma (0.78, 0.15 to 3.97) and seizure (2.21, 0.69 to 7.07) included 1. These are counts of people who became ill and were reported, not rates in people who take MDMA: sodium was recorded in only 35 in 100 of the cases, and the authors say that spectrum bias, incomplete laboratory data and differences between individuals prevent determining causality. The paper gives neither the amount of fluid drunk nor the amount of MDMA taken. The only comparison read of women and men given the same amount is described second-hand in a 2020 narrative review (Faria et al., 2020): in a randomized placebo-controlled crossover study, 8 healthy men and 8 healthy women were given 125 mg of MDMA in a laboratory (study conditions), and copeptin, a marker of the water-holding hormone, rose in the women but not in the men, while no significant differences were seen in the hormone itself or in blood sodium. The direction is the same, without a test, in the UK series in which 10 of 17 patients and both who died were female (Hartung et al., 2002), in an earlier series of 18 cases with 17 women that the California paper cites and that was not read, and, as described in a narrative review (Campbell & Rosner, 2008; second-hand), in more than 85 in 100 of published symptomatic cases, whose table draws 10 rows from the California series and so is not independent; the 2020 review's table of published cases (1991 to 2018) lists 46 women among 52 rows (the review's 89 in 100), from which it infers that women are predisposed, but the table appears to count two patients twice (44 of 50, 88 in 100, editors' calculation), cites an unrelated laboratory-methods paper for one woman's case, draws 10 of its 21 deaths from the California series and sets no case count against the number of women and men who take MDMA. These series are of young people (mean age 21 in California; 15 to 26 in the UK series), so age cannot be compared. Reasons the authors and the reviews offer (metabolic and hormonal factors; oestrogen effects on water retention and on the brain's response to low sodium; lower muscle mass and body weight) were not tested in people who took MDMA; the 2020 review's main support for a greater risk to women once the brain swells comes from patients after surgery, among whom women who still menstruated were about 25 times more likely than men or women past menopause to die or have lasting brain injury (Ayus et al., 1992, as described in the review).
claims.magnitude: California poison control, people with ecstasy intoxication and a recorded sodium (Rosenson): low sodium (below 130 mmol/L) in 55 of 105 women (52.4%) and 18 of 83 men (21.7%), odds ratio 3.97 (95% CI 2.08 to 7.59); of the 73 with low sodium, 55 (75.3%) were women, against 296 of 545 (54.3%) women among all cases. Sodium was recorded in 35.3% of women and 33.3% of men. Within each sex, low sodium against not: coma 3.93 (1.20 to 12.90) in women and 0.78 (0.15 to 3.97) in men; seizure 4.38 (1.74 to 11.00) and 2.21 (0.69 to 7.07); death 1.39 (0.22 to 8.65) and 1.85 (0.16 to 21.70). Editors' calculation: 31 more in 100 women than men had low sodium among those tested (52.4 minus 21.7). UK series (Hartung): 10 of 17 patients and both deaths female. Earlier series cited by the California paper (not read): 17 of 18 women; 2 of 3 in an Israeli series of 32. Narrative review (Campbell), second-hand: more than 85% of published symptomatic cases female. Narrative review (Faria), second-hand: 46 of 52 tabulated cases women (89%; without two probable duplicates 44 of 50, 88%, editors' calculation); laboratory crossover, 8 men and 8 women given 125 mg MDMA: copeptin rose in women but not in men, no significant differences in ADH or sodium; postoperative patients with hyponatraemic encephalopathy (Ayus et al., 1992): menstruant women about 25 times as likely to die or have permanent brain injury as men or postmenopausal women. No rate in women or men who take MDMA can be derived.
